 Brain tumors: What to know, who’s at risk and when to see a doctor
 Published 2:23 am Monday, November 16, 2026
 by
 Providence Regional Medical Center Everett 
 Dr. Martin Holland, MD, chief of neurosurgery and medical director of neurosciences development at Providence Regional Medical Center Everett. 
 A neurosurgeon explains the four paths after diagnosis and the team approach behind every treatment plan 
 Two patients can hear the words “brain tumor” in the same week and face entirely different futures. One may be sent home with a plan for repeat scans. The other may be in surgery within days. 
 That range is the first thing patients should understand, says Dr. Martin Holland, MD, chief of neurosurgery and medical director of neurosciences development at Providence Regional Medical Center Everett . 
 “Not all tumors are created equal. Some are benign, some are malignant, some start in the brain or skull and others travel there from somewhere else,” Dr. Holland says. “Different tumors require different treatments and sometimes the right treatment is no treatment at all.” 
 Symptoms depend on where a tumor sits. Tumors on the hearing nerve can cause hearing loss in one ear. Tumors of the pituitary gland may show up as hormone or vision changes.  
 Certain tumors lead to weakness or a loss of motor skills. Because first-time seizures in adults commonly trigger an urgent evaluation to check for a brain tumor, medical attention is typically sought right away.  
 Headaches, however, present a more complex picture.  
 “A tumor is always there, so when it irritates the brain the headache tends to be constant,” Dr. Holland says. “If a headache is always in the same spot, never fully goes away or gets progressively worse, that’s worth a conversation with your doctor.” 
 Brain and spinal tumors are treated by a team of four full-time neurosurgeons at Providence Everett. The team serves patients from King County to the Canadian border.
 Risk climbs with age. Most brain tumors are diagnosed in people in their 50s through 80s, and they are less common under 40.  
 Family history matters too, particularly when several relatives have had tumors, which can point to a genetic syndrome.  
 What happens after a suspected diagnosis 
 A CT scan offers a fast first look, while an MRI provides the detail surgeons need, and most patients get both. From there, the path depends on the tumor’s type, its location and how likely it is to grow or cause symptoms. A biopsy and repeat scans often guide that decision. 
 Treatment generally follows one of four main avenues – monitoring, surgical removal, radiation, or chemotherapy – with many patients receiving a combination of these approaches. 
 A team approach, close to home 
 Brain and spinal tumors are treated by a team of four full-time neurosurgeons at Providence Everett. Among them, Dr. Holland offers specialized expertise in skull base surgery, utilizing endoscopic techniques via nasal access. 
 “We can perform a textbook perfect surgery, but that means nothing without the rest of the team,” Dr. Holland says. “In most cases the surgery is just the beginning.” 
 His clinic sits inside the cancer center, and a tumor board of pathologists, oncologists and radiation specialists meet twice a month to review cases together.  
 The team serves patients from King County to the Canadian border. 
 “One of the most important parts of the job is managing expectations and hope,” Dr. Holland says. “You never want to take away all hope.”
